title: Tools of good works (Rule 4)
hookLine: a long list of tools, ending: never despair of God's mercy
tomorrow: why would Benedict ration even the good words?

cards: Plenty of notes apps hold a list called something like be a better person: drink water, call Grandma, stop scrolling at midnight.
Chapter four of Benedict's Rule is that list, for a monastery, and he calls the items tools. Love the Lord God with all your heart. Visit the sick.
Bury the dead. Don't return evil for evil. Love your enemies.
Don't be a grumbler. Keep death daily before your eyes. Tool after tool.

teach.b: Benedict calls them the instruments of good works, the tools of the spiritual craft. A carpenter doesn't use every tool at once; she picks up the one the job needs.
Some come straight from the Gospels: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself. Some are small: don't love much talking, make peace with an opponent before the sun goes down.

And the workshop, he says, is the monastery, and staying put in one community. Now, Christians have a real conversation about lists like this. One side says a rule of life is how faith becomes a life.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: TOOLS GIVE LOVE HANDS.
teach.b: Without tools, love stays a feeling; with them, it gets hands. That's why some Christians, monks and others, keep a rule of life. The other side worries that a list turns into a scorecard.
They hear Paul: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."

teach.h: THE OTHER: LISTS CROWD OUT GRACE.
teach.b: A checklist, they say, can crowd out grace, and leave a person either proud or crushed.

teach.h: THE LAST TOOL IS A GIFT.
teach.b: Here's what's worth telling a friend: Benedict's last tool sits right where those two views meet.
The list is real work, and it ends on a gift. Anyone who picks it up will drop something. The last tool keeps them from throwing the whole toolbox away.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Benedict, and Benedict asks that the Rule be read aloud often in the community; chapter four's tools are part of that reading.

games.q: what does “tools of good works” mean?
o: a list of good deeds that earn a place in heaven
carpentry tools the monks used to build the monastery
Benedict's list of practical habits for a life with God

games.q: tools of good works — tap the pairs.

s: Benedict expected every tool to be used, perfectly, all at once
the skimmer's reading. like a carpenter, you pick up the tool the job needs.
Benedict's list of tools ends with never despair of God's mercy
he saves it for last, for the days the other tools slip.
Benedict says the workshop is the monastery and staying in one community
the tools work where you actually live, with the people you live with.

games.q: you love lists. your friend says a faith checklist always turns into a scorecard. what's her best case, in her own terms?
o: lists are only for people who don't really love God.
a list can crowd out grace, and leave you proud or crushed.
Benedict's tools were only ever meant for monks.
games.why: that's the real worry, built on Paul: by grace, not of works. and Benedict's own list ends on mercy, the place where both views meet.

practice: Pick one tool from the list: visit the sick, make peace before sundown, don't grumble. Name one place this week it would help, name what usually gets in the way, and plan the moment you'll reach for it.
If you pray, you can end on Benedict's last tool: never despair of God's mercy.

wordCard.voice: Tools of good works. Benedict's list of small, practical instruments for a life with God, ending with mercy.

orig.note: Latin for tools or instruments: Benedict calls the chapter the instruments of good works.

carryVoice: Your line: never despair of God's mercy. It's the tool Benedict left for last, for the days the others slip. See you tomorrow.
